title: NAU-CSC 111/NAU-SEN: Proof Strategy, Types of Proof Strategy
subject: NAU-CSC111/NAU-SEN 111
description: A practice CBT exam for NAU-CSC 111/NAU-SEN

questions.question: In a proof by 'Contraposition,' to prove P → Q, we assume:
questions.explanation: In a proof by contraposition, instead of proving P → Q directly, you prove the logically equivalent ¬Q → ¬P. So you begin by assuming ¬Q (i.e. Q is false), then derive ¬P (i.e. P is false). Option A (assume P true) is the direct-proof opening. Option B (assume Q true) is the converse Q → P, not the contrapositive. Option D (assume P false) is the inverse ¬P → ¬Q. The golden rule: assume the negation of the conclusion, derive the negation of the premise.

questions.question: Which method is used to prove that √2 is irrational?
questions.explanation: The classic proof that √2 is irrational proceeds by contradiction: assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms (i.e. p and q have no common factor), derive p² = 2q², which forces both p and q to be even — contradicting the assumption that they share no common factor. Option A (induction) is for statements indexed by naturals. Option C (direct proof) starts from √2's definition but cannot derive irrationality directly. Option D (construction) builds objects to prove existence — irrelevant here.

questions.question: The 'Base Case' in induction is required to prevent:
questions.explanation: Without a base case, an induction argument is just a chain of implications (P(1)→P(2), P(2)→P(3), …) with nothing anchoring it — the chain never actually starts, leading to infinite regress. The base case verifies P(1) (or P(0)), giving the chain a starting point. Option B (circular logic) is a distinct fallacy: assuming what you want to prove. Option C (tautologies) and Option D (antisymmetry) are unrelated concepts.

questions.question: A 'Non-constructive' existence proof typically utilizes:
questions.explanation: A non-constructive existence proof shows that an object exists without producing it. It often uses the Law of Excluded Middle (every proposition is either true or false) to argue "it must be one way or the other" without committing to which. Options A (algorithms), C (direct computation), and D (examples) are all constructive — they exhibit or compute the object, which is exactly what non-constructive proofs avoid.

questions.question: Providing a single instance where a universal claim fails is a proof by:
questions.explanation: A counterexample is a single specific instance that falsifies a universal statement. To disprove "all P are Q," it suffices to exhibit one P that is not Q. Option A (cases) and Option B (exhaustion) are positive proof methods. Option D (paradox) is a self-contradictory statement, not a disproof technique. The magic of a counterexample: one example is enough to destroy a universal claim, whereas proving it requires an argument covering every case.

questions.question: In a 'Proof by Contradiction,' if we wish to prove P → Q, we begin by assuming:
questions.explanation: To prove P → Q by contradiction, assume both P and ¬Q — the antecedent is true but the consequent is false, i.e. the negation of the whole implication ¬(P → Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q. Then derive a contradiction. Option A (P ∧ Q) is what you would be trying to conclude, not assume. Option C (¬P → ¬Q) is the inverse, not the negation. Option D (¬P ∨ Q) is equivalent to P → Q itself — assuming it would be circular.

questions.question: The 'Contrapositive' of the statement 'If n² is even, then n is even' is:
options: If n is even, then n² is even
If n is odd, then n² is odd
If n² is odd, then n is odd
n is even and n² is odd
questions.explanation: The original is P → Q with P = "n² is even" and Q = "n is even". Its contrapositive is ¬Q → ¬P = "n is not even → n² is not even" = "n is odd → n² is odd". Option A (n even → n² even) is the converse (Q → P), which is not equivalent to the original. Option C (n² odd → n odd) is the inverse (¬P → ¬Q), also not equivalent. Option D is a conjunction, not an implication. Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original — this is exactly why we can replace the original with it in a proof.

questions.question: Which proof method is specifically designed to prove statements over the set of all Well-Ordered integers?
questions.explanation: Mathematical induction relies on the fact that the natural numbers (and any well-ordered set) have a least element and no infinite descending chains. That structural property is what makes the base case + inductive step sufficient. Option B (exhaustive proof) checks every case — impossible for infinite sets. Option C (constructive existence) proves one object exists, not a statement for all n. Option D (direct inference) is a general logical technique, not induction-specific.

questions.question: In the 'Inductive Step' of a proof, we prove that:
options: P(n) is true for all n
questions.explanation: The inductive step proves the implication P(k) → P(k+1) for an arbitrary integer k — "if it holds at k, it holds at k+1." Option A (P(1)) is the base case. Option B (P(k)) is the inductive hypothesis, an assumption you make at the start of the inductive step, not what you prove. Option D (P(n) for all n) is the conclusion you draw after finishing both the base case and the inductive step.

questions.question: A 'Non-Constructive Existence Proof' establishes that an object exists without:
options: Using logical reasoning to prove it
questions.explanation: A non-constructive existence proof shows that an object exists without producing it — for example, by contradiction ("if it didn't exist, we'd get a contradiction"). Option A is wrong because the proof is still a logical argument (just not a construction). Option C is wrong: the proof must still be consistent. Option D is subtly different — "not providing an algorithm" is a consequence, but the definitional point is that no explicit witness is constructed.

questions.question: Which proof method relies on the fact that if (¬Q → Contradiction) is true, then Q is true?
questions.explanation: This is proof by contradiction — assume ¬Q, derive a contradiction (something impossible), conclude Q. The logical form is ¬Q → (R ∧ ¬R) ⟹ Q. Option A (direct proof) goes from premises to conclusion without assuming the negation. Option B (contrapositive) proves ¬Q → ¬P rather than reaching a contradiction. Option D (induction) is a completely different structure.

questions.question: In Mathematical Induction, the 'Inductive Hypothesis' involves assuming the statement holds for:
questions.explanation: The inductive hypothesis assumes the statement P holds for some arbitrary integer k — this is the "suppose" in "suppose it holds at k." Option A (n=1) is the base case. Option C (n=k+1) is what you prove in the inductive step. Option D (all n) is the conclusion — assuming it would be circular reasoning.

questions.question: To disprove a 'For all x, P(x)' statement, one must provide a:
questions.explanation: To disprove ∀x P(x), it suffices to find a single x for which P(x) is false — a counterexample. This works because ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x): the negation of "all" is "at least one not." Option A (tautology) is a statement always true, not a disproof. Options B and D are positive proof methods, useless for disproof.

questions.question: A 'Constructive' proof of existence:
questions.explanation: A constructive existence proof exhibits or builds the object whose existence is claimed — you actually produce a witness. Option A (assume it exists) is circular. Option C (contrapositive) is a technique that may or may not be constructive. Option D (uniqueness) is a different kind of claim — it shows at most one object satisfies the property, not that one exists.

questions.question: Which strategy proves P → Q by instead proving ¬Q → ¬P?
questions.explanation: Proving ¬Q → ¬P instead of P → Q is proof by contrapositive — a form of indirect proof. (Caution: the phrase "indirect proof" is used in some textbooks to mean contradiction, not contrapositive. Here it is explicitly qualified with "(Contrapositive).") Option B (vacuous proof) proves P → Q by showing P is always false. Option C (cases) splits into subcases. Option D (trivial proof) proves P → Q by showing Q is always true regardless of P.

questions.question: Which proof starts by assuming P is true to conclude Q?
questions.explanation: A direct proof of P → Q assumes P is true and derives Q through logical steps — "hypothesis to conclusion." Option A (indirect) begins with ¬Q and derives ¬P. Option C (contradiction) assumes P ∧ ¬Q and derives any contradiction. Option D (induction) is for universally quantified statements over well-ordered sets.

questions.question: Proof by contrapositive proves P → Q by showing:
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of P → Q is ¬Q → ¬P, and the two are logically equivalent. Option A (Q → P) is the converse. Option B (¬P → ¬Q) is the inverse. Option D (P ∧ ¬Q) is the negation of P → Q — assuming it would be proof by contradiction's opening, not contrapositive. Only ¬Q → ¬P is the correct equivalent form.

questions.question: In proof by contradiction, we assume the statement is:
questions.explanation: In proof by contradiction, we assume the statement is false (i.e. its negation is true) and derive a contradiction — showing the negation cannot hold, so the original must be true. Option A (assume true) would be begging the question. Options C and D describe syntactic forms of statements, not what you assume.

questions.question: Mathematical induction is primarily used to prove statements about:
questions.explanation: Mathematical induction is used for statements indexed by natural numbers (or any well-ordered set): P(1), P(2), P(3), … Option A (reals) is not well-ordered — there is no "next real number" after 0, so induction cannot step. Option C (complex numbers) has no natural ordering. Option D (empty sets) is a single trivial case, not a domain for induction.

questions.question: The first step in mathematical induction is the:
questions.explanation: Every induction argument begins with the base case — verify the statement for the smallest value (usually n = 0 or n = 1). Option A (inductive step) comes after the base case. Option B (recursive step) is computer-science terminology for a related idea but not the standard proof term. Option D (conclusion) is the final claim after both steps.

questions.question: Which proof strategy assumes P is true and uses logical steps to derive Q?
questions.explanation: This is direct proof — assume the antecedent P, apply definitions, axioms, and known theorems, and derive the consequent Q. Option A (indirect) begins with ¬Q. Option C (contradiction) begins with P ∧ ¬Q. Option D (counterexample) is a disproof technique, not a proof technique.

questions.question: Proof by Contrapositive is based on the logical equivalence:
questions.explanation: The defining equivalence is P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P. Option A (¬P → ¬Q) is the inverse — not logically equivalent. Option B (Q → P) is the converse — not logically equivalent. Option D (P ∧ ¬Q) is the negation of the implication, which is what proof by contradiction assumes. Only the contrapositive is a valid substitute for the original.

questions.question: Which method is used to disprove a universal statement by finding one instance where it fails?
questions.explanation: Proof by counterexample disproves a universal claim by exhibiting a single instance where it fails. It exploits ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). Options A, B, and D are all positive proof methods — they establish truths, not refute them.

questions.question: In Mathematical Induction, the first step is to prove the statement is true for an initial value. This is called the:
questions.explanation: The base case verifies the statement for the starting value (often n = 1 or n = 0). Option A (inductive step) proves the implication P(k) → P(k+1). Option C (inductive hypothesis) is the assumption P(k) inside the inductive step. Option D (conclusion) is the final "therefore P(n) is true for all n." Order matters: base case first, then inductive step.

questions.question: A proof that establishes the truth of a statement by assuming it is false and reaching an impossibility is:
questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction assumes the statement is false (its negation), derives an impossibility (a contradiction), and concludes the statement must be true. Option A (contrapositive) proves ¬Q → ¬P, not "assume false and hit a contradiction." Option B (direct) works forward from premises. Option D (existence) proves something exists — sometimes via contradiction, but that is a specific use, not the general method.

questions.question: What is a proof?
options: A guess that a statement is true or false by intuition
A logical argument that establishes the truth
A test with examples to show that something is true
questions.explanation: A proof is a logical argument that establishes the truth of a statement beyond any reasonable doubt, using definitions, axioms, and previously proved results. Option A (intuition) is unreliable — intuition fails all the time in mathematics. Option C (testing examples) can never prove a universal statement; it can only suggest one or provide a counterexample. Option D (opinion) is not a proof at all — mathematics is not a matter of vote.

questions.question: What is a proof strategy?
options: A random attempt to prove something
An organized plan to prove something
A list of theorems that proves something
A computer program that checks proofs
questions.explanation: A proof strategy is an organized plan or method for demonstrating that a mathematical statement is true (or false). It selects the appropriate technique — direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction, cases — based on the shape of the statement. Option A (random) is the opposite of strategic. Option C (list of theorems) is not a plan. Option D (program) is a proof checker, a tool, not a strategy.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a basic component of a proof?
questions.explanation: The basic components of a proof are premises/assumptions, definitions, axioms/postulates, lemmas, theorem statements, and the conclusion. A counterexample is not a component — it is a disproof tool used to refute universal claims. Options A, B, and D are all legitimate components of a proof.

questions.question: What is an axiom?
options: A statement that has been proven
An intermediate result used to prove larger results
questions.explanation: An axiom (or postulate) is a statement accepted as true without proof — a starting point for reasoning. Examples: "through any two distinct points there is exactly one line" (Euclidean geometry); "for every a, a = a" (equality). Option A (proven statement) is a theorem. Option C (intermediate result) is a lemma. Option D is the theorem/claim being proved.

questions.question: What is a lemma?
options: A statement that has been proven
An intermediate result used to prove larger results
questions.explanation: A lemma is a small theorem proved along the way to help prove a bigger result — a "helper theorem." Often its only purpose is to make the main proof cleaner. Option A (proven statement) is a theorem. Option B (accepted without proof) is an axiom. Option D is the target theorem. Example: "Euclid's Lemma" (if a prime p divides ab, then p divides a or p divides b) is used to prove the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

questions.question: In a direct proof of "If P, then Q", what do you assume first?
questions.explanation: In a direct proof of P → Q, you assume P is true and use definitions, axioms, and known theorems to derive Q. Option A (assume Q) is circular — you cannot assume the conclusion. Option C (assume ¬P) is the inverse approach. Option D (assume ¬Q) is the start of contrapositive or contradiction.

questions.question: What is the logical basis for proof by contrapositive?
questions.explanation: Contrapositive relies on the equivalence P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P. Option A (Q → P) is the converse — not equivalent. Option C (¬P → ¬Q) is the inverse — not equivalent. Option D (P ∧ ¬Q) is the negation of P → Q. Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent, which is why proving it proves the original.

questions.question: In a proof by contradiction, what do you assume?
questions.explanation: In proof by contradiction, you assume the statement is false — i.e. assume its negation — and derive a contradiction. Having shown the negation leads to impossibility, the original must be true. Option A is circular. Options C and D describe statement forms, not assumptions.

questions.question: Proof by cases involves which of the following?
options: Proving a statement by assuming it is false
Dividing a problem into several exhaustive cases
Proving a statement by finding one example
Proving a statement using mathematical induction
questions.explanation: Proof by cases splits the situation into exhaustive cases (covering every possibility) and proves the statement separately in each. Example: to prove something about integers, split into "n is even" and "n is odd." Option A describes contradiction. Option C describes existence proof by example. Option D describes a different method entirely. The key word for cases is exhaustive — the cases must cover all possibilities, or the proof has a gap.

questions.question: What is the base case in mathematical induction?
options: Assume the statement is true for n = k
Prove the statement is true for n = k+1
Prove the statement is true for the initial value
questions.explanation: The base case proves the statement for the initial value — usually n = 1 or n = 0, sometimes n = 2 or another starting point. Option A (assume at k) is the inductive hypothesis. Option B (prove at k+1) is the inductive step. Option D (assume false) belongs to proof by contradiction.

questions.question: What is the inductive hypothesis in mathematical induction?
options: Prove the statement is true for the initial value
Assume the statement is true for n = k
Prove the statement is true for n = k+1
Prove the statement is true for all n
questions.explanation: The inductive hypothesis is the assumption that the statement holds for some arbitrary n = k. From this assumption you derive P(k+1) in the inductive step. Option A (initial value) is the base case. Option C (prove at k+1) is the inductive step. Option D (prove for all n) is the conclusion you earn after both steps.

questions.question: What is the inductive step in mathematical induction?
options: Prove the statement is true for the initial value
Assume the statement is true for n = k
Prove the statement is true for n = k+1
Prove the statement is true for n = 0
questions.explanation: The inductive step proves P(k) → P(k+1): given the inductive hypothesis at k, derive the statement at k+1. Option A is the base case. Option B is the inductive hypothesis. Option D is a specific case of the base case (for n = 0). Together with the base case, the inductive step gives P(n) for all n.

questions.question: What is a constructive existence proof?
questions.explanation: A constructive existence proof explicitly constructs or exhibits the object whose existence is claimed — you produce a witness. Option A describes non-constructive existence. Option C (uniqueness) shows at most one object satisfies the property — different claim. Option D (disproving a universal) is a counterexample, a disproof method.

questions.question: What is a non-constructive existence proof?
questions.explanation: A non-constructive existence proof shows the object exists without constructing it — often by contradiction or by the Law of Excluded Middle. Classic example: "there exist irrational a, b such that aᵇ is rational" — proved without identifying which pair works. Option A (construct) describes a constructive proof. Options C and D are unrelated claims.

questions.question: What is a uniqueness proof?
options: Shows that a particular object exists
Shows that exactly one object satisfies a given property
Disproves a universal statement by giving a false scenario
Proves that at least one object exists that satisfies a property
questions.explanation: A uniqueness proof shows that exactly one object satisfies the given property. The standard structure is: (i) prove existence (at least one), then (ii) suppose two objects x and y both satisfy the property and prove x = y. Option A proves only existence, not uniqueness. Option D proves only the "at least one" part. Option C is a counterexample.

questions.question: What is a proof by counterexample?
options: Proves a universal statement by showing that it cannot fail in any situation
Disproves a statement by finding a single example where it fails
Proves an existential statement by giving an example of such an object
Proves a statement by contradicting and hitting a dead end
questions.explanation: Proof by counterexample disproves a universal claim by producing a single specific instance where it fails. Option A describes how you would prove a universal claim (not disprove it). Option C describes a constructive existence proof — proving an existence claim by example, which is different. Option D describes contradiction, not counterexample.

questions.question: What strategy is recommended for an implication (P → Q)?
questions.explanation: For an implication P → Q, the two most natural strategies are direct proof (assume P, derive Q) and contrapositive (assume ¬Q, derive ¬P). Option A includes induction, which is for universally quantified statements over naturals, not implications in general. Option C (constructive) is for existence claims. Option D (counterexample) disproves, it does not prove.

questions.question: What strategy is recommended for a universal statement?
questions.explanation: For a statement of the form ∀n P(n), the recommended strategies are direct proof (if P(n) can be shown for arbitrary n) or mathematical induction (if P(n) has a recursive structure over naturals). Option A is for implications. Option C is for existence claims. Option D disproves universal claims.

questions.question: What strategy is recommended for an existence claim?
questions.explanation: For a statement of the form ∃x P(x), the recommended strategy is constructive proof — exhibit an x that satisfies P(x). Option A (direct proof) is for implications. Option B (contrapositive) is for implications. Option D (counterexample) disproves universal claims, the opposite of an existence claim.

questions.question: What strategy is recommended for the negation of a universal claim?
questions.explanation: The negation of ∀x P(x) is ∃x ¬P(x). To prove this existence claim, you produce a specific x for which P(x) fails — a counterexample to the original universal. The strategy is called "counterexample" because that is exactly what you are producing, even though strictly it is a constructive existence proof for the negation. Options A, B, and C are all positive proof methods that assume the claim to be proved — they do not naturally fit a negated universal.

questions.question: What strategy is recommended for a complex condition?
questions.explanation: For a statement with a complex condition — often a disjunction or a property that naturally splits into sub-types — the recommended strategy is proof by cases: break the condition into exhaustive sub-cases and prove each. Option A (direct) works only when the condition is simple enough to handle in one pass. Option B (contrapositive) suits implications. Option D (induction) suits naturals. Cases is the go-to when a single argument would be tangled, but each case is manageable.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common mistake in proof writing?
options: Assuming what is to be proven
questions.explanation: Assuming what is to be proven — circular reasoning (petitio principii) — is one of the most common proof-writing errors: you use the conclusion as a premise somewhere along the way. Options A, C, and D are all good practices, not mistakes: use definitions precisely, state the conclusion clearly, and provide every logical step. Other common errors include skipping steps, using examples instead of a general argument, and confusing contradiction with contrapositive.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common mistake in proof writing?
options: Using examples instead of general proof
questions.explanation: Clearly stating definitions is good practice — it grounds the proof and helps the reader follow the argument. Options A (skipping steps) makes the proof unverifiable. Option B (examples as proof) can never establish a universal claim. Option C (confusing contradiction and contrapositive) leads to incorrect logical structure. Only D is a virtue, not a vice.

questions.question: Which of the following is an importance of proof strategies in computer science?
questions.explanation: Proof strategies underpin multiple areas of computer science: verifying algorithm correctness (e.g. proving sorting routines terminate and produce sorted output), proving properties of data structures (e.g. that a balanced tree remains balanced after operations), and formal reasoning in AI (e.g. automated theorem provers, knowledge representation). They also appear in software and hardware verification (model checking, type systems). All three listed options are genuine applications.

questions.question: In the proof that if n is an even integer, then n² is even, what is the first step?
options: Assume n is even, so n = 2k for some integer k
questions.explanation: This is a direct proof of "n even → n² even," so the first step is to assume the hypothesis: n is even, so n = 2k for some integer k. Then n² = (2k)² = 4k² = 2(2k²), which is even (twice an integer). Option B (assume n² even) is the conclusion — circular. Options C and D would be the opening of a contrapositive proof of the opposite statement ("n² odd → n odd"), not of this one.
